title: Improving soil with an organic waste pit
summary: We improve poor soil by adding plant remains and organic waste. An organic waste pit turns rubbish into manure.
body:
## Where soil needs help

Look around your school or home for soil that needs improving:

- **Bare, hard ground** where nothing grows
- Places where **water runs off** and washes soil away
- Gardens where crops look **yellow and weak**

## Organic waste pit

An **organic waste pit** is a hole where we put things that rot, so they turn into manure.

1. Dig a pit about **1 metre long, 1 metre wide and 1 metre deep** in a corner of the garden.
2. Put in **organic waste**: leaves, peelings, weeds without seeds, animal droppings.
3. Cover each layer with a little **soil** to keep away flies and smells.
4. Keep it **damp** but not waterlogged.
5. After 2–3 months, dig out the dark manure and spread it in the garden.

**Never** put plastics, glass, metals or batteries in the pit.

## Using plant remains

- **Mulching**: spread dry grass or maize stalks on the soil. Mulch keeps moisture in, stops weeds and rots into manure.
- **Dig in** bean and pea leaves after harvest — they add nutrients to the soil.
activities:
1. Walk around your home. Find one spot where soil needs improving and say why.
2. Separate organic and non-organic waste at home for one day.
3. Mulch one row of crops or one flower bed with dry grass.
reflection: How does an organic waste pit keep the compound clean as well as improve the soil?

quiz.question: What does mulching do?
Which can go into an organic waste pit?
Why cover each layer with soil?
options: To keep away flies and smells

quiz.question: Which sign shows soil needs improving?

title: Listening for the main idea
summary: Every talk or story has a main idea and supporting details. Careful listeners find both and respond.
body:
## Main idea and details

- The **main idea** is what the whole text is mostly about.
- **Details** are the smaller facts that support it.

Listen to this:

> *Water is precious. We use it for drinking, cooking and washing. Farmers need it for crops and animals. In dry seasons, many families walk long distances to fetch it. That is why we must never waste water.*

- **Main idea:** Water is precious, so we must not waste it.
- **Details:** we drink and cook with it; farmers need it; some walk far to fetch it.

## Clues to the main idea

- It is often in the **first or last sentence**.
- Words that are **repeated** (water, water, water).
- The speaker's **tone** — what they stress.

## Responding

After listening, you can:

- **Summarise** in one sentence.
- **Ask a question:** *"How can we save water at school?"*
- **Give your opinion:** *"I think every school should harvest rainwater."*
activities:
1. Listen to the news on radio or TV. Write the main idea of one story in one sentence.
2. Read the water passage to someone. Ask them for the main idea.
3. Write two ways your family can save water.
reflection: Why is it useful to know the main idea before you remember the details?

quiz.question: What is the main idea of the water passage?
options: Water is precious, so we must not waste it

quiz.question: Where is the main idea often found?
options: In the first or last sentence

quiz.question: Which is a detail from the passage?

title: Matamshi bora: f/v, s/z, l/r, th/dh
summary: Tunatofautisha sauti f/v, s/z, l/r na th/dh ili tutamke maneno kwa usahihi na kudumisha maana.
body:
## Sauti zinazokaribiana

| Sauti | Mifano |
|---|---|
| **f / v** | **f**una – **v**una, **f**ua – **v**ua |
| **s / z** | **s**aa – **z**aa, **s**ima – **z**ima |
| **l / r** | **l**ala – **r**ara, **l**angi – **r**angi |
| **th / dh** | **th**amani – **dh**ahabu, **th**eluji – **dh**ambi |

Mifano ya maana:

- **Vuna** mahindi (kukusanya mavuno) si **funa**.
- Taa **imezimika**, si **imesimika**.
- **Rangi** ya nyumba ni nyeupe.

## Vitanzandimi

- *Fatuma alivua viatu akafua vitambaa vya Vumilia.*
- *Zuhura na Saida wanasaga mtama sasa hivi.*
- *Rehema alilala kando ya ziwa la rangi ya kijani.*

## Vitendawili

- *Popo mbili zavuka mto.* — **Macho.**
- *Ajenga ingawa hana mikono.* — **Ndege.**
activities:
1. Tamka maneno kwenye jedwali kwa sauti. Mwombe mtu akusikilize.
2. Kariri kitanzandimi kimoja mara tatu bila kukosea.
3. Unda kitanzandimi kipya kwa sauti l na r.
reflection: Neno gani lilibadilisha maana zaidi likitamkwa vibaya?

'Saa' na 'zaa' zinatofautiana kwa sauti...

strand: Living things and their Environme nt
title: Flowering and non-flowering plants
summary: Some plants have flowers and make seeds in fruits; others do not. Each part of a flower has a job.
body:
## Two groups of plants

| Flowering plants | Non-flowering plants |
|---|---|
| Have flowers, make seeds inside fruits | Have no flowers |
| Maize, beans, mango, hibiscus, sunflower | Ferns, mosses, pine (seeds in cones) |

## Parts of a flower

| Part | Job |
|---|---|
| **Petals** | Bright colours and scent attract insects and birds |
| **Sepals** | Green leaf-like parts that protect the bud |
| **Stamen** (anther and filament) | Makes **pollen** (male part) |
| **Pistil** (stigma, style, ovary) | Receives pollen; the **ovary** grows into a fruit with seeds (female part) |

## Pollination

Bees and butterflies visit flowers for nectar. Pollen sticks to them and is carried to another flower. This is **pollination**, and it lets the flower make seeds.

## Why flowers matter

- They give us **fruits and seeds** to eat.
- Bees make **honey** from nectar.
- Flowers make our homes and gardens beautiful, and some are sold for money — Kenya exports roses all over the world.
activities:
1. Collect a flower that has fallen. Find the petals, sepals, stamen and pistil.
2. Make a table: list 5 flowering and 2 non-flowering plants near your home.
3. Watch a flowering bush for 10 minutes. Which insects visit it?
reflection: What would happen to our food if there were no bees?

title: The elements of a map
summary: A good map has a title, frame, key, compass and scale. These help us read and understand it.
body:
## What is a map?

A **map** is a drawing of a place as seen **from above**, on a flat surface.

## Key elements of a map

| Element | What it tells us |
|---|---|
| **Title** | What the map shows, e.g. *"Map of Kilifi Town"* |
| **Frame** | A border around the map |
| **Key** (legend) | What each **symbol** means |
| **Compass** | Directions — North is usually at the top |
| **Scale** | How a distance on the map compares with the real distance on the ground |

## Symbols in a key

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| ✚ | Hospital |
| ⛪ | Church |
| 🕌 | Mosque |
| ━━ | Road |
| 〰 (blue) | River |

## Scale

A scale of **1 cm : 1 km** means every 1 cm on the map is 1 km on the ground. Two towns 5 cm apart on the map are **5 km** apart.
activities:
1. Draw a sketch map of your school with a title, frame, key, compass and scale.
2. Make your own symbols for a market, a borehole and a bus stage.
3. Look at a map in a book. Name two symbols and say what they mean.
reflection: Which map element would help you most if you were lost in a new town?
